  • Estimated population, July 1, 2025: 430,324 (Census Bureau).

What are your options for selling a house fast in Minneapolis?

Minneapolis owners choose between an agent listing, a sale without an agent and a direct sale to a cash buyer. Whichever route you take, a house, duplex or townhouse in the city needs a Truth in Sale of Housing report before anyone can be shown through it, so that step shapes the schedule more than the choice of buyer does.

Census Bureau figures for 2025 show 430,324 residents spread over 54 square miles of land. Owners live in 47.7% of homes, which means plenty of Minneapolis houses change hands between investors, landlords and first-time buyers as well as long-term owners. Time on market, repair costs and a report that must be filed before showings are the practical variables to weigh.

  • Agent listing: the widest exposure, though showings wait for the city report to be filed and displayed.
  • Sale by owner: the same city report applies, and you handle disclosures and paperwork yourself.
  • Cash sale: the buyer takes the house in its present condition, and the report still has to exist for the transfer.

What does Minneapolis require before a house can be shown?

The city requires a Truth in Sale of Housing (TISH) evaluation for single-family houses, duplexes, townhouses and first-time condominium conversions, and the full report must exist before you show the property. The requirement covers sales by owner, sales through an agent, advertising a home for sale, contracts for deed and other title transfers, according to the city's TISH page.

You hire an evaluator licensed by Minneapolis. Evaluators are not city employees and set their own prices, so comparing quotes is reasonable. The evaluator inspects the building inside and outside, writes the disclosure report and files it online where you and the city can both see it.

A report stays valid for two years or one sale, whichever ends first. You must keep a copy on display so prospective buyers can read it at showings. A separate pre-inspection report does not replace it.

Two situations skip the evaluation: a property holding a Certificate of Code Compliance (issued when a house comes out of condemnation, good for up to one year) or a Certificate of Occupancy for a newly built home (good for one sale).

What happens if the report lists repairs?

If the evaluator lists required repairs, you can complete them and receive a Certificate of Approval online, or sell with the repairs open and pass them to the buyer. When the work is still undone at closing, the buyer signs an acknowledgement of responsibility, and the city asks for that form within one business day of closing. The buyer then has 90 days after closing to finish the repairs.

Before you book the evaluation, the city suggests reviewing its list of commonly required repairs and fixing what you can, since fixed items will not appear on the report. After the buyer completes the work, either an evaluator or a city inspector reinspects, and a successful result brings a Certificate of Completion.

  • Seller with all repairs finished: Certificate of Approval, no acknowledgement form needed.
  • Seller with repairs open: buyer signs the acknowledgement and owns the 90-day deadline.
  • Buyer who later resells: must finish the repairs and obtain a new report first.

For a seller with a dated house, this is the main cost question. The city office for these reports is Minneapolis Truth in Housing, reachable at 612-673-5840.

What do Census figures say about Minneapolis homes?

The Census figures below show what a typical Minneapolis household pays to own or rent, and how long the commute runs.

Minneapolis housing snapshot, Census Bureau QuickFacts, 2020-2024 unless noted
MeasureMinneapolis
Typical home value (owner-occupied)$362,200
Share of homes lived in by owners47.7%
Median gross rent$1,371
Monthly owner cost, mortgaged homes$2,128
Households192,734
Average commute22.0 minutes

Those are citywide medians. A bungalow near one of the lakes and a duplex on a busy corridor can sit far from the middle, so use them as context and not as an appraisal.

How do Hennepin County property taxes affect a Minneapolis sale?

Hennepin County collects Minneapolis property tax in two halves, due May 15 and October 15, and a 15th that falls on a non-business day slides to the next business day. Statements go out in March, and valuation notices also arrive in March showing how the property was assessed as of January 2.

That timing matters when you sell. A sale in summer leaves the second-half bill still ahead, and the assessment you see in March sets next year's tax. Hennepin's overview explains that your share depends on the assessor's value, how the property is classified and the levies of the taxing districts that cover it, and that more than 70 local governments levy in the county. The county's property tax line is 612-348-3011.

  • January 2: the assessor's value and classification date.
  • March: valuation notices and tax statements mailed.
  • May 15 and October 15: the two payment dates.

Your purchase agreement decides who covers the current year's bill, so ask the title company how it will be apportioned.

What else should a Minneapolis seller consider?

The city's 2040 Comprehensive Plan ended single-family-only zoning citywide, and the Minnesota Legislature approved it in 2024 after court challenges. A buyer evaluating your lot may ask what the zoning would allow, so ask the city's planning staff before you answer.

Minnesota law also requires a written seller disclosure before you sign a purchase agreement. Under Minnesota Statutes 513.55, you list material facts you know that could significantly affect an ordinary buyer's use and enjoyment, and the disclosure must be made in good faith. A leaking basement, a past sewer backup or an unpermitted addition belongs there.

Winter timing is real. The record for snowfall in one Minneapolis winter is 98.6 inches (1983 to 1984), and summers run hot and humid, so exterior photos, roof condition and drainage are easier to show in spring and fall. The city has 83 neighborhoods, and buyers often search by neighborhood and by distance to light rail, which the Metro Blue and Green lines provide.

When does a cash sale make sense in Minneapolis?

A cash sale tends to suit owners facing a deadline, an inherited house, tenants who will not leave, or repairs that a TISH report would make visible. In those cases the buyer purchases the house as it stands, and the open repair items move to the new owner through the acknowledgement process.

Compare any offer to what the same house would net after listing costs, a repair list and carrying costs while it sits. Ask who pays for the evaluation, how the buyer handles the city paperwork and when funds arrive. You can also request a written offer with no obligation and a firm closing date.

More questions about Minneapolis, MN

Do I need a Truth in Sale of Housing report to sell my Minneapolis house?

Yes for most houses. Single-family houses, duplexes, townhouses and first-time condominium conversions need the report before the property is shown. A Certificate of Code Compliance or a Certificate of Occupancy for a new build can replace it.

How long is a Minneapolis TISH report good for?

Two years or one sale, whichever comes first. A buyer who finishes any open repairs must obtain a new report before reselling.

Who pays for repairs listed on the city report?

The purchase agreement decides. If repairs remain open at closing, the buyer signs an acknowledgement of responsibility, files it within one business day, and finishes the work within 90 days.

What dates does Hennepin County set for Minneapolis property tax?

May 15 and October 15. When either lands on a weekend or holiday, you have until the next business day.

Can I sell a Minneapolis house that needs major repairs?

Yes. The report must still be filed and displayed, but you are allowed to sell with required repairs outstanding if the buyer accepts them and signs the acknowledgement. A cash buyer often takes that route.

Last updated November 14, 2026.

St. Paul at a glance

  • Estimated population, July 1, 2025: 306,684 (Census Bureau).
Selling in St. Paul?

What should I know before selling a house in St. Paul?

St. Paul adds a step that most Minnesota cities lack: a city-licensed evaluator must inspect most one- and two-unit homes before the listing goes live. The city calls it Truth-in-Sale of Housing, or TISH, and it applies to single-family houses, duplexes, condominiums and townhomes.

The rest of the process looks like a sale anywhere in the state. You sign a disclosure, record a deed in Ramsey County and settle taxes at closing. Your route (agent listing, owner sale or a direct cash offer) changes the timeline more than the paperwork. The sections below cover the St. Paul rules first, then the neighborhood and housing facts that shape pricing.

What does St. Paul look like by the numbers?

The Census Bureau estimates 306,684 people lived in St. Paul on July 1, 2025. That is 1.5% fewer than the 311,503 April 2020 base, so the capital city shrank slightly while Woodbury and Sherburne County grew.

  • 125,249 households averaging 2.37 people (2020 to 2024)
  • 52.9% of homes owner-occupied, so nearly half of the housing stock is rented
  • Median value of an owner-occupied home: $294,500
  • Median monthly owner cost with a mortgage: $1,911
  • Median gross rent: $1,281
  • Median household income: $73,394, with 43.8% of adults 25 and older holding a bachelor's degree

Those figures explain why many St. Paul sellers hold rental or inherited property. A house that sat as a rental for years often has deferred repairs, and the TISH report will record them for buyers.

Who needs a Truth-in-Sale of Housing report, and when?

Owners of single-family homes, duplexes, condominiums and townhomes need a TISH evaluation before the home is marketed for sale. Buildings with three or more units, commercial buildings and mixed-use buildings are outside the program. A condominium with its own Ramsey County parcel number still needs a report even when the building holds a certificate of occupancy, because that certificate only covers common areas.

The report must be available to any prospective buyer within three calendar days of listing. It stays good for 365 days and covers one sale by the owner named on it. If your offer is accepted inside that year, closing can fall after the expiration date without a new report.

The evaluator is a private contractor licensed by the city, and the evaluator sets the fee. The city does not recommend anyone. Call the Department of Safety and Inspections at 651-266-8989 before you list if you are unsure whether your sale needs a report.

What does the TISH report actually require me to fix?

Very little. The report is disclosure only, and the single mandatory item in a single-family house is a working hard-wired smoke alarm. If the evaluator marks it as a hazard, the city's electrical inspector sends a letter and you must hire a licensed electrical contractor to pull a permit and install the alarm. The contractor then calls the inspector to close the permit.

Everything else on the report informs the buyer and does not force a repair. Sellers who want to avoid hazard marks can fix items first, and the city publishes a list of the ten most common deficiencies for that purpose. Failing to follow the program is a misdemeanor under Chapter 189 of the Saint Paul Legislative Code.

Which sales are exempt from TISH?

The table lists the main rules from the city's Truth-in-Sale of Housing page.

Truth-in-Sale of Housing rules, as listed on the City of Saint Paul Safety and Inspections page
QuestionAnswer
Covered propertiesSingle-family, duplex, condominium, townhome
Not coveredThree or more units, commercial, mixed-use
Deadline to have report on handWithin three calendar days of listing
Report validity365 consecutive days, one sale
Accepted substitutesCertificate of Code Compliance or current Certificate of Occupancy
Family exemptionGrandparents, parents, children, grandchildren, siblings
Vacant buildingsCategory 1 needs a report before sale; Categories 2 and 3 need a code compliance inspection

Aunts, uncles and cousins do not count as immediate family under the program. The same page requires a smoking policy disclosure form when you sell a unit in a condominium, townhome or similar community, a rule that took effect January 1, 2022.

How do St. Paul's rent rules affect a rental house I want to sell?

They matter to your buyer more than to you, but they affect what the property is worth. Voters approved a rent stabilization ordinance on November 2, 2021, and the City Council amended it in September 2022 and May 2025. Rent increases are capped at 3% in a 12-month period unless an exception applies.

  • Self-certification: available for increases from 3% to 8%, evaluated each year
  • Just cause vacancy: the consumer price index change plus 8%, after city review
  • Staff determination: no fixed limit when the landlord justifies the figure
  • Separate tracks exist for new construction and for low-income housing providers

A tenant-occupied house therefore comes with limits on how fast the next owner can raise the rent. Vacant houses give a buyer more room, which is one reason investors look at emptied rentals. If tenants live in the home, ask the city's Rent Stabilization team at 651-266-8553 how the rules apply to your unit.

What shapes the housing stock across St. Paul?

Water and hills explain most of the map. The city grew at the junction of the Mississippi and Minnesota Rivers, on bluffs the glaciers cut, and it covers 56.18 square miles, of which 51.98 are land. The city planning office divides the area into 17 planning districts, and each has a council that weighs in on land use.

Older neighborhoods near downtown and along the river carry homes from the steamboat and railroad eras. The 1904 storms that damaged hundreds of downtown buildings and the 1960s freeway work, which cleared the Rondo neighborhood for Interstate 94, both left marks on where houses stand today. On the south side, the former Ford assembly plant site in Highland Park is being redeveloped as Highland Bridge, planned with about 3,800 housing units.

Winters are cold and snowy, and the city expects more spring and summer rain over time, which can lead to river and flash flooding. Buyers and inspectors in St. Paul look hard at basements, roofs and drainage for that reason.

How do transit, schools and parks affect a St. Paul sale?

Getting around is easy by Twin Cities standards. Interstates 94 and 35E cross the city, along with US 52 and Minnesota 280 and 5. The METRO Green Line runs along University Avenue to Minneapolis, the A Line serves arterial streets, and Amtrak's Empire Builder stops at Union Depot.

The city runs 160 parks and 41 recreation centers, and a 2018 ranking placed its park access second nationally behind Minneapolis. Saint Paul Public Schools is the state's largest district, and families can also use charter schools, private schools and open enrollment. Macalester College, the University of St. Thomas, Hamline University and Saint Catherine University all sit within the city, which keeps demand steady for houses near campuses.

What closing steps apply to a St. Paul house sale?

Minnesota requires a written disclosure of material facts about the property before you sign a sale agreement, under Minnesota Statutes 513.55. The disclosure must be made in good faith and reflect what you know.

The deed gets recorded where the property sits, which for St. Paul is Ramsey County. Ask the Ramsey County recorder for current recording fees and ask your title company who files the paperwork. Keep your TISH report, any smoke alarm permit and repair receipts together so your closing agent can pass copies to the buyer.

A direct sale to a cash buyer changes the schedule but the city rules above still apply to the property. Ask Safety and Inspections whether a report is needed before you accept an offer.

More questions about St. Paul, MN

Do I need a TISH report to sell my St. Paul house?

Yes, if it is a single-family home, duplex, condominium or townhome and the sale is not to immediate family. Buildings with three or more units are exempt. The report must be on hand within three calendar days of listing.

How long is a TISH report valid?

It is valid for 365 consecutive days and covers one sale by the owner named on it. If a seller accepts an offer within that year, closing may fall afterward without a new report.

What is the one repair TISH can force?

A working hard-wired smoke alarm in single-family homes. If one is missing or not working, the city sends a letter and a licensed electrician must install one under a permit.

Does Ramsey County or the city record my deed?

Ramsey County records deeds for St. Paul property. The city handles the TISH report, rental rules and permits, so you deal with two offices during a sale.

Can I sell a house with tenants in St. Paul?

Yes. Existing leases continue under the rent stabilization rules, which cap increases at 3% a year unless an exception is granted. Call the city's Rent Stabilization team at 651-266-8553 for questions about your unit.

Rochester at a glance

Where is Rochester, Minnesota, and what should a home seller know about the city?

Rochester, the Olmsted County seat, lies in the bluff country of southeast Minnesota, 85 miles from the Twin Cities. Its hills rise around the south fork of the Zumbro River, on the edge of a Driftless Area that glaciers never covered, and its 56.8 square miles of land make it a spread-out city.

George Head built a log tavern here in 1854 and named the settlement for his hometown in New York. The Winona and St. Peter Railroad arrived in October 1864, and after the 1883 tornado flattened much of the town, the Sisters of St. Francis opened St. Marys Hospital in 1889 with the Mayo family's help. Olmsted is one of only four Minnesota counties with no natural lake, so the water you see in town, such as Silver Lake, was made by damming the river.

As of July 1, 2025 the Census Bureau puts Rochester at 124,292 residents. That is 2.4 percent more than in April 2020 and about 17,500 more than the 2010 count of 106,769, which makes it Minnesota's third largest city.

Rochester measure, 2020-2024 Census estimatesFigure
Households51,131
Homes lived in by their owners65.1%
Median value of an owner-occupied home$310,500
Median monthly owner cost with a mortgage$1,864
Median gross rent$1,399
Median household income$89,389
Average trip to work17.4 minutes

How does the Rochester economy affect the housing market?

Medicine drives it. Mayo Clinic started in Rochester, and 2022 Economic Census receipts for health care and social assistance came to about $2.98 billion, beside roughly $3.40 billion in retail sales. Workers in those fields, plus the students at the University of Minnesota Rochester and Rochester Community and Technical College, keep a steady stream of renters and first-time buyers in the market.

The state's Destination Medical Center plan, signed in 2013, is meant to channel a multibillion dollar Mayo investment into downtown districts such as Discovery Square and Heart of the City. Construction near the river and the medical campus can change the feel of a nearby block, so a seller close to downtown should expect buyers to ask about it.

Not every owner has time for a retail listing. Typical situations in a university and hospital town include:

  • a relocation after a residency, fellowship or job change;
  • a rental left behind by a tenant who moved out;
  • a house inherited from a relative who lived in another state;
  • an older home with deferred repairs that would be expensive to fix before listing.

What do Rochester winters, wind and storms mean for an older house?

Rochester's climate is warm-summer humid continental, with around 33 inches of rain and nearly 52 inches of snow in a typical year. Wikipedia lists it as the second windiest city in the country, with winds averaging 12.6 mph, and the January to April stretch is the windiest.

Severe weather has left a record. Two F4 tornadoes hit the city in 1953 and 1962, a June 2010 tornado damaged homes around the Lincolnshire neighborhood on the northwest side, and a June 2019 storm hit southwest Rochester. A 1978 flood led the city to rework nearby rivers and streams for flood control.

  • Roof and siding that have taken years of wind are the first things an inspector looks at.
  • Basements near the Zumbro and its creeks deserve a moisture check before you list or accept an offer.
  • Frozen-pipe damage in a vacant house is a real winter risk, so keep the heat on during a sale.

A buyer paying cash usually takes a storm-worn house as it stands, which spares you the repair bids.

How do roads, transit and schools shape a Rochester sale?

Three U.S. highways cross the city: U.S. 14, U.S. 52 and U.S. 63. Interstate 90 and State Highway 30 skirt the southern edge, and downtown buildings are tied together by skyways and underground walkways that people use to stay out of the cold. Rochester International Airport is seven miles south of downtown, with flights to Atlanta, Chicago, Denver and Minneapolis.

A 2.6 mile bus rapid transit line called Link, planned along 2nd Street Southwest, is listed for an August 2027 opening. Homes within walking distance of that corridor may draw different questions from buyers than homes in the outer ring.

Rochester Public Schools divides the city into John Marshall, Mayo and Century high school zones, and Lourdes and Rochester Central Lutheran School are private alternatives. Ask the district which zone an address falls in before it goes into a listing.

What must a Rochester landlord do before selling a rental house?

Anyone renting out a dwelling in Rochester needs a Rental Housing Certificate under city ordinance chapter 7-3-2, including a single-family house the owner does not live in. The city says renting without one is a misdemeanor punishable by up to a $1,000 fine, 90 days in jail, or both.

  • Certificates renew each year, and the fee depends on the number of units.
  • Inspection scores set a one, two, three or four year cycle, and a compliant inspection is required in the year it is due.
  • A certificate must be transferred within 30 days of a property sale, and the city has a termination form for owners who have sold.
  • A building that sits vacant must be registered within 30 days under ordinance 7-14-6, and an annual vacant building fee follows.

Short stays of up to 30 days follow separate rules. A second home listed on a rental platform needs a Short Term Rental license and a compliant inspection, while an owner-occupied room rental needs registration. For questions, the Community Development office is at 4001 W. River Parkway NW, Suite 100, and the city's main line is 507-328-2311.

When are Olmsted County property taxes due, and who pays at closing?

Olmsted County lists May 15 and October 15, 2026 as the real estate installment dates, with farm parcels on a later November 16 date. A house owner has no more 2026 installments to pay, and the next bill comes due in May 2027.

For a sale during the year, the county describes a proration at closing. The seller owes tax from January until closing day, and the buyer owes it from closing through December 31. A seller who prepaid the entire year is repaid for the buyer's part. Mid-year buyers get no mailed statement, and the county warns that a missing statement is no defense for a late payment.

After a sale the county mails the new owner a homestead application. Return it, because the homestead classification determines the value exclusion that lowers the tax bill. Questions go to the county's revenue and records line at 507-328-7636.

How can I appeal my Rochester property value?

Begin with evidence, meaning recent appraisals or sales of comparable houses, and take it to the Assessor's Office (507-328-7670, Property Records, 151 4th Street SE). Unresolved disputes go to the meetings printed on the valuation notice, local board first where one exists and the county board where it does not.

Past that, the Minnesota Tax Court takes petitions once the valuation notice has arrived, with an April 30 cutoff in the year the tax is payable. Olmsted County will accept a petition served by email, or in person at the County Attorney's Office on Fourth Street Southeast.

The 2026 appeal calendar has closed, so a change to the 2026 value is no longer available to you. The next notices arrive in the spring.

What are the transfer and disclosure steps when a Rochester house sells?

Minnesota's state deed tax is 0.33 percent of net consideration, and a deed with a price of $3,000 or less pays a flat $1.65 (Minn. Stat. 287.21). It falls due the moment the deed reaches the recorder. Ask Olmsted County Property Records and Licensing how it wants deeds submitted.

State law adds a radon step ahead of any signed sale agreement: the seller discloses test results and any mitigation system in writing and hands over the Department of Health booklet on radon in real estate (Minn. Stat. 144.496). Transfers to heirs are exempt.

More questions about Rochester, MN

Can I sell a Rochester house without fixing it first?

Yes, to a buyer who accepts it as-is. Material facts you know about still go to the buyer in writing (Minn. Stat. 513.55), and a landlord should settle the rental certificate and inspection status before taking an offer on an occupied rental.

Do I need to tell a buyer about radon?

Yes. Minnesota requires a written radon disclosure before you sign an agreement to sell residential property, and a seller who withholds known radon facts can be sued within two years after closing. The disclosure covers any tests, reports and mitigation system you know about.

What happens to my rental certificate when I sell a Rochester rental?

It has to be transferred within 30 days of the sale, and the city offers a termination form for owners who have sold. Contact Community Development at 507-328-2311 so the certificate does not stay in your name.

Who pays property tax on the day a Rochester house closes?

The county says the seller pays from January to the closing date and the buyer pays from closing to December 31. If the seller prepaid the whole year, the buyer repays the seller for the buyer's part at closing.

Is it too late to appeal this year's Rochester assessment?

For the 2026 value the county meetings are over. Only a Minnesota Tax Court petition remains, due by April 30 of the payable year, and the next valuation notice opens a fresh round.

What must a Bloomington seller do before listing a house?

Before you list, show or sell a house in Bloomington, the city requires a Time-of-Sale housing inspection and a filed evaluation report. The rule covers single and two-family dwellings, condominiums, townhouses and mobile homes, and it applies to private sales as well, including a sale to a family member that is never listed. Multi-family rental buildings of four or more units are left out.

This requirement is the biggest difference between selling here and selling in most Minnesota suburbs, so it shapes the whole timeline. Cash buyers purchase as-is, but the city's inspection step still applies to the sale. The rest of this page walks through what the inspection costs, what it can force you to fix and who can take on a hazard.

How does the Bloomington Time-of-Sale inspection work?

The owner or listing agent schedules the inspection with the city's Building and Inspections Division at 952-563-8930 or through an online request form, and the evaluator needs about 120 minutes on site. The fee is $250, which includes the energy disclosure and any re-inspections, plus a service fee of $1.95 for an e-check or 2.95 percent for a card. If you cancel before a site visit, the city offers a refund of up to 50 percent within 60 days of your request.

  • The evaluator examines visible structure, heating, electrical and plumbing, and accessible attics and crawl spaces, and does not take anything apart.
  • The report does not cover lead paint, radon or asbestos, and it does not guarantee the home.
  • The report must be displayed at the house and given to the buyer before or at sale, and a copy must reach the city within 7 calendar days.
  • The report and the Certificate of Compliance are good for one year and only for the owner named on them.

Since April 2022 the inspection has included an energy disclosure covering the heating and cooling system, water heater, insulation and windows, and the city says no energy upgrades are required of the seller.

What counts as an immediate hazard, and who pays to fix it?

Only nine categories of defect must be corrected, and the seller is responsible unless the buyer agrees in writing to take them over. The city lists them as unsafe heating systems, unsafe water heaters, dangerous electrical conditions, unsanitary plumbing, structures unable to carry their loads, roofs, walls and foundations that are not weather tight, abandoned fuel tanks, unsanitary refuse or infestation, and missing or non-working smoke detectors.

Other defects are noted in the report but do not have to be repaired. If hazards are found, a re-inspection by a city inspector is required before the house can be occupied, and the owner or contractor must pull any permits. A buyer who is willing to take the hazards must get the city's written consent by signing a Hazard Correction/Responsibility form, which is currently handled through DocuSign by calling the same 952-563-8930 line. The Certificate of Compliance is typically required at closing.

Which sales are exempt from the Bloomington inspection?

Five kinds of transfer are exempt, but you must still call the city to say which exemption you are using. They are a newly built dwelling transferred to its first owner, a multiple dwelling already licensed as rental, a sale to a public body, a sale for demolition, and a sale by a sheriff or other court officer. The last exemption does not cover a sale by someone appointed by a probate court, which matters for heirs selling an inherited Bloomington house.

If your sale does not fit an exemption, plan for the inspection and the report date before you set a closing. Check any open work permits as well, because the owner or contractor must obtain the necessary permits and the dwelling is subject to re-inspection of open permits before occupancy.

What do Bloomington's housing figures show?

Bloomington is a mid-priced suburb in which 65.7 percent of homes are owner-occupied and the median home value is $361,700. The table compares the figures a seller uses to sense-check a price.

Source: Census Bureau QuickFacts for Bloomington. The same-house rate is 87.5 percent, and 19.8 percent speak a language other than English at home.

What is Bloomington like, and who shops for homes here?

Bloomington is the largest suburb in the Twin Cities, with 89,034 people, 10 miles south of downtown Minneapolis on the north bank of the Minnesota River. It was settled in 1843, the Town of Bloomington was incorporated on May 11, 1858, and it became a city on November 8, 1960. The postwar housing boom filled in much of the street grid you see today.

Interstate 35W divides the city informally. West Bloomington is mostly residential with newer housing, while East Bloomington has more industry, retail and the less expensive housing. Highway 77 (Cedar Avenue), Highway 169 and Interstate 494 frame the rest of the map, and the Metro Blue Line light rail runs from the Mall of America to downtown Minneapolis and both airport terminals.

The employer base is strong. Mall of America tenants are the largest group, with Dayforce, Donaldson, Great Clips, HealthPartners and Toro headquartered here. ISD 271 runs fifteen public schools, with John F. Kennedy High School in the east and Thomas Jefferson High School in the west, and the attendance line runs near France and Xerxes Avenues. A buyer will ask which side of that line you are on.

Which city fees and bills should a seller check before closing?

Before closing, call the city to find out whether anything is owed on the property, because outstanding items are easier to clear before the title company asks. The city's Time-of-Sale page lists the right numbers.

  • Assessing Division: 952-563-8722, for fees or fines associated with the property.
  • Utility Billing: 952-563-8726, for the current outstanding water bill.
  • Environmental Health: 952-563-8934, for pending civil fines.
  • Finance: 952-563-4527, for pending weeds, trees, brush removal and abatements.

Hennepin County bills the property tax, due May 15 and October 15, and it takes recordings by appointment, online through its Virtual Recorder site with a $3 service fee, by mail or through eRecording for title companies. Its recording page lists a $46 fee per document and a $54 well disclosure certificate when one is needed, and it says properties with delinquent taxes cannot be transferred under Minnesota Statute 272.12. Minnesota Statute 513.55 separately requires a written seller disclosure before the purchase agreement is signed.

More questions about Bloomington, MN

Is the Bloomington inspection required for a cash sale?

Yes, it applies to any sale of a covered dwelling, cash or financed, listed or private. The only way out is one of the five exemptions in city code, and you still have to call the city to say which one applies.

Do I have to repair everything the Bloomington inspector finds?

No. Only the nine immediate hazard categories must be corrected, and the buyer can assume them with the city's written consent. Other deficiencies are listed in the report without a repair requirement.

How long is a Bloomington Time-of-Sale report valid?

One year from the date of issue, and only for the owner named on it.

Who gets the Certificate of Compliance?

The city sends it to the owner or listing agent once no hazards remain. It is typically required at closing, so ask your agent or title company to confirm they have it before the signing date.

Can an heir selling an inherited house in Bloomington skip the inspection?

Usually not. The sheriff and court-officer exemption does not apply to a sale by a person appointed by a probate court, so a personal representative should plan for the inspection and report.

Duluth at a glance

Selling in Duluth?

Where is Duluth and how does the hillside shape the city?

Duluth is a port city on the western tip of Lake Superior and the county seat of St. Louis County. It covers 71.69 square miles of land, and the Census Bureau estimates 88,330 residents as of July 1, 2025, which makes it one of Minnesota's largest cities.

The city climbs a steep hillside from the lakeshore to the plateau above, and the population hugs the shoreline, so Duluth runs mostly southwest to northeast. The weather station at Sky Harbor Airport on Minnesota Point sits at 607 feet, while Duluth International Airport on top of the hill is at 1,427 feet. Skyline Parkway runs along the ridge from above the Gary and New Duluth area to Lester Park, and neighborhoods such as Piedmont Heights and Bayview Heights sit up top with long views. Over the hill, the Miller Hill Mall area and the big-box strips along the Miller Trunk Highway corridor form a separate retail center.

For a seller, the steep streets and elevation changes make the exact address matter more than it does in a flat suburb.

What is the history behind Duluth?

The Ojibwe name for the area is Onigamiinsing, or Misaabekong. The city takes its name from Daniel Greysolon, Sieur du Lhut, the first known European explorer of the St. Louis River, in 1679. Fur traders worked the Fond du Lac area through the early 1800s, and the American Fur Company set up its headquarters at present-day Fond du Lac in 1817.

The 2020 census counted 86,697 people, which ranked Duluth fifth among Minnesota cities. By land area it is second in the state, behind only Hibbing. Duluth and Superior, Wisconsin, share a metropolitan area known as the Twin Ports.

What drives the Duluth economy?

Duluth serves as the regional center for health care, higher education, retail and business services across northeastern Minnesota and nearby parts of Wisconsin and Michigan. The Census Bureau recorded $3.1 billion in health care and social assistance receipts in the city for 2022.

  • The Port of Duluth handles about 35 million short tons of cargo and nearly 900 vessel visits a year, including coal, iron ore, grain, limestone and wind turbine parts.
  • The University of Minnesota Duluth enrolled 9,253 students in 2024, Lake Superior College 5,607 and the College of St. Scholastica 2,930.
  • Tourism leans on Canal Park, the Aerial Lift Bridge, the North Shore drive and access to the Boundary Waters.
  • Maurices, the women's clothing chain, is headquartered here.

Most public school students attend Duluth Public Schools, Independent School District 709. The Proctor Public School District covers a small part of southwest Duluth, and Duluth Edison Charter Schools serve kindergarten through grade 8.

How does Duluth weather affect an older house?

Duluth has a humid continental climate moderated by the lake, and winters are long. Highs stay at or below 32 degrees for about 100 days a year, temperatures fall to 0 or below on 38 nights, and snow cover lasts from late November to early April. Average snowfall is 90.2 inches, and lake-effect storms can leave a foot or more near the shore while places 50 miles inland get much less.

The first freeze usually arrives around September 30 and the last around May 14. The record low is minus 41 degrees, set in 1885, and July days average about 78 degrees. A house here carries a heavy load from snow, ice and freeze-thaw cycles, so roofs, gutters, foundations and insulation draw attention from buyers and inspectors.

What have Duluth home prices and days on market looked like?

The city's 2024 Housing Indicator Report tracks sales of single-family homes, and the table shows the trend since 2021.

Duluth single-family median sale price and average days on market. Source: City of Duluth 2024 Housing Indicator Report.

In 2024 there were 1,195 single-family listings and 1,033 sales. Foreclosures in Duluth ran 16 in 2020, 8 in 2021, 30 in 2022, 34 in 2023 and 20 in 2024. The Census Bureau puts the owner-occupied rate at 59.4 percent, the median value of owner-occupied homes at $242,700 and median gross rent at $1,087. Median household income is $68,807, and the poverty rate is 16.8 percent.

Which Duluth housing and building codes apply to a sale?

Duluth keeps its housing rules in the city's Legislative Code, and several chapters touch a sale.

  • Chapter 29A covers housing, property maintenance and rental licensing. The Life Safety Division of the Fire Department administers it, and it adopts the 2012 International Property Maintenance Code.
  • Chapter 30 covers abandoned property and inoperable vehicles.
  • Chapter 50, the Unified Development Code, is the zoning code.
  • Chapter 10 adopts the Minnesota building code, and the 2020 edition took effect in Duluth on March 31, 2020.

Rental owners should know that about 17,633 units held active rental licenses in 2024 and that 39.4 percent of households rent. Construction Services and Inspections is at 411 West First Street, Room 100, and the phone number is 218-730-5240. If the house had a fire, note that Duluth withholds fire escrow funds under Minnesota Statutes 65A.50, so ask the city what applies before you accept an offer.

Can a Duluth vacation rental permit transfer to a buyer?

No. Duluth requires a city permit to rent any part of a property on Airbnb, Vrbo or similar sites, and existing vacation dwelling units are not transferable to another owner. An Interim Use Permit lasts six years or until ownership changes, whichever comes first.

There are three kinds of permit. An Accessory Home Share Permit applies when the owner lives in the building and allows stays of 1 to 29 nights, with up to 4 guests in 2 bedrooms. An Accessory Vacation Dwelling Unit, Limited Permit covers an owner-occupied homestead rented for 2 to 7 nights, to a maximum of 21 nights a year. Interim Use Permits allow 2 to 29 nights, a local property manager and no more than 9 guests. Those permits are subject to a city-wide cap outside the form districts, and the city says the current waiting list is expected to take several years. A buyer who wants income from short stays should confirm eligibility with Planning at 218-730-5580 before closing.

What does St. Louis County handle in a Duluth sale?

The St. Louis County Recorder and Registrar of Titles handles deeds and certificates of title. About two-thirds of documents recorded there involve abstract property and about one-third involve Torrens property, so ask your title company which kind you have. The county does not offer legal advice or help preparing documents.

Minnesota's state deed tax is 0.33 percent of net consideration under Minnesota Statutes 287.21, so a sale at the 2024 median price of $295,000 carries about $974 in tax. You also owe the buyer written disclosure of material facts under Minnesota Statutes 513.55.

County property tax is due May 15 and October 15. The 2026 second half has passed, so the next payment is May 15, 2027. Value appeals start with the assessor, then the city board of appeal and equalization in April or May, then the county board in the last two weeks of June, and a Minnesota Tax Court petition must be filed by April 30 of the year the tax is payable.

What are your choices for selling a house in Duluth?

You can list through an agent, sell the house yourself, or take a direct cash offer, and the best route depends on repairs, timing and what the house is used for.

With average time on market at 19 days in 2024, a well-prepared Duluth listing can move quickly. A cash sale suits a vacation rental owner who cannot transfer a permit, a landlord ending a license, a house with winter damage, or an estate that needs to close without repairs. Compare any offer with the median sale price, ask for the terms in writing, and keep your tax, permit and disclosure paperwork in one folder.

More questions about Duluth, MN

Can I sell my Duluth Airbnb with its permit?

No. The city says existing vacation dwelling units cannot transfer to another owner, and an Interim Use Permit ends when ownership changes or after six years. A buyer must apply under the city's rules, and Planning at 218-730-5580 can explain the current cap and waiting list.

What was the median home sale price in Duluth in 2024?

The median single-family sale price was $295,000, up from $282,350 in 2023. Average time on market was 19 days, according to the city's 2024 Housing Indicator Report.

What happens to insurance money on a fire-damaged Duluth house?

Duluth withholds fire escrow funds under Minnesota Statutes 65A.50. Contact Construction Services and Inspections at 218-730-5240 to learn what applies to your property before you sign a sale agreement.

How do I appeal my Duluth property value?

Start by contacting the St. Louis County assessor. If you are not satisfied, appear before the city board of appeal and equalization in April or May, then the county board in the last two weeks of June, and file in Minnesota Tax Court by April 30 of the year the tax is payable.

Does winter make it harder to sell a house in Duluth?

Snow cover usually lasts from late November to early April, and the average snowfall is 90.2 inches, so showings happen in tough conditions. Clear walks and roofs, keep the driveway plowed and have heating and insulation records ready, since buyers look closely at winter performance.

Which selling routes make sense in Brooklyn Park?

Three routes cover nearly every Brooklyn Park sale: a listing with an agent, a private sale, or a cash purchase by an investor. Match the route to the condition of the house and to how many weeks you can spare.

  • A listing reaches the most buyers and tends to produce the strongest price. It also brings showings, inspection requests, and a closing date tied to the buyer's lender.
  • A private sale keeps the commission-side savings in your pocket, and puts pricing, forms and negotiation on you.
  • A cash purchase is quickest. Buyers take the house as it stands, which helps with inherited homes, deferred maintenance and tenant-occupied properties, and the price reflects that convenience.

All three end the same way, with a deed recorded in Hennepin County, so the closing notes below apply whichever you pick.

What kind of city is Brooklyn Park for a home seller?

Brooklyn Park is the sixth-largest city in Minnesota, a suburb on the west bank of the Mississippi River in northern Hennepin County. It covers about 26 square miles of land, with the river forming its eastern edge opposite Coon Rapids and Fridley, and it uses ZIP codes 55428, 55429, 55443, 55444 and 55445.

Settlers from Michigan organized the town government in 1858 and named it after their hometown of Brooklyn, Michigan. The township became a village in 1954 and a city in 1969. Population climbed from 26,230 in 1970 to 86,478 in 2020, and the Census Bureau's July 2025 estimate is 83,543, a 3.4% drop from the 2020 base. Land north of 85th Avenue was mostly developed after 2000, so one street map can show 1960s houses beside houses barely two decades old.

The city still has farmland, including the historic Eidem Homestead working farm. It is a Tree City USA with 67 parks and 47 miles of trails, among them Rush Creek Regional Trail, part of Palmer Lake Park and Mississippi Gateway Regional Park.

How do the roads, climate and commute look to a buyer?

Interstate 94 and Interstate 694 run through the far south of Brooklyn Park, US 169 is near the west side, MN 252 runs near the east side, MN 610 crosses the north, and County Road 81 is a main local route. Workers spend a mean of 21.3 minutes getting to their jobs, a short drive for the metro.

Winters are real. The January average high is about 23 degrees Fahrenheit, July averages near 83, and the city receives about 25 inches of precipitation a year. A buyer's inspector will look hard at the roof, the attic insulation and the furnace, so service records for those items are worth gathering before you list.

How do Brooklyn Park home values and incomes look?

Owners hold 70.3% of the homes in Brooklyn Park. For 2020-2024 the median owner-occupied value was $336,200, median gross rent was $1,325, and median household income was $89,891.

  • 29,148 households, averaging 2.86 people each.
  • 91.3% of residents were in the same house a year earlier, which points to low turnover.
  • 25.8% of residents are foreign-born, and 31.8% of people age 5 and up speak a language other than English at home.
  • The 2020 census counted 29,656 housing units, 3.1% of them vacant, with a rental vacancy rate of 5.5%.

The same census found children under 18 in 38.7% of households and a median age of 35. For a seller, that profile means growing families who care about school boundaries, a garage and a yard.

Which school districts serve Brooklyn Park?

Three districts cover the city: Osseo Area Schools (District 279) for most addresses, Anoka-Hennepin (District 11), and Robbinsdale (District 281). The street decides which one applies, so verify it before you write a listing.

Osseo Senior High and Park Center Senior High are in the Osseo district, Champlin Park High belongs to Anoka-Hennepin, and Cooper High belongs to Robbinsdale. Families can also use Minnesota's open enrollment to send children to a school in a different district. Rasmussen University, North Hennepin Community College and a Hennepin Technical College campus are all in the city.

Where do Brooklyn Park residents work?

Manufacturing is the largest job category in Brooklyn Park, followed by health care and retail. The figures below come from the city's 2023 annual financial report, which counts 33,176 jobs.

Largest job sectors in Brooklyn Park, 2023

Manufacturing8,23824.83%

Retail trade3,51310.59%
Educational services2,8208.50%

The Census Bureau's 2022 retail sales total for the city is about $6.5 billion, more than twice the $2.9 billion reported for Burnsville.

What rules apply if the next owner will rent the house out?

A rental license is required for any single-family dwelling in Brooklyn Park that is not owner-occupied. The exception is a home rented to an immediate family member who is granted a relative homestead exemption. No more than four unrelated people may live in the home.

Rental properties are inspected, and the inspection, including any repairs, must be completed before the license can be renewed. The city may deny, suspend or revoke a license over noisy parties, illegal drugs, weapons, assault or other criminal behavior. The license holder or designated operator must attend a one-day Crime-free Housing class within a year. The rule is in Chapter 117.40 of the city code, and the Rental and Business Licensing Division is at 763-493-8182.

This matters when you sell to an investor. The buyer needs the license in place before a tenant moves in, and a house with open maintenance issues will draw a longer inspection list.

What does closing look like in Hennepin County?

The Hennepin County Recorder files the buyer's deed at the Government Center in Minneapolis, and most title companies handle that step on closing day. The file typically includes these pieces:

  • Deed tax of 0.33% of net consideration under Minnesota Statutes section 287.21, collected at recording. For a $336,200 sale the tax is about $1,109.
  • An eCRV number, needed whenever the price is above $3,000.
  • The $5 agricultural conservation fee on taxed deeds, plus a $46 recording fee for the document.
  • Well information: either a well disclosure certificate with a $54 fee or a statement on the deed.
  • Clear tax status. A parcel with delinquent taxes cannot be transferred.

You can record by appointment on the seventh floor of the A-tower, by mail, through eRecording for title firms, or on the county's Virtual Recorder site, which adds a $3 service fee. Electronic filings post in one to three business days, and mailed originals come home within one to two weeks.

What must a Brooklyn Park seller disclose?

Minnesota wants a written statement from you before the purchase agreement is signed. It must cover the material facts you know that could adversely and significantly affect the buyer's use and enjoyment of the property (section 513.55), made in good faith from your best knowledge at that moment.

If the house came through an estate or sat vacant, record what you do know: past water in the basement, roof repairs, and work done without a city permit. Brooklyn Park inspects rentals for smoke alarms, carbon monoxide alarms within ten feet of bedrooms, handrails on stairs with four or more steps, and working plumbing, so a former rental sells more smoothly when those items are fixed.

More questions about Brooklyn Park, MN

Can a damaged Brooklyn Park house still be sold?

Yes. Investors and cash buyers purchase houses with roof, foundation or interior damage, and owners also sell them on the open market at a lower price. Known material problems must still be disclosed in writing.

Who files the deed after a Brooklyn Park closing?

The Hennepin County Recorder, normally by way of the title company. The submission includes the eCRV number, deed tax at 0.33% of the price, the $5 conservation fee and a well certificate or well statement.

Is a license needed before I lease my house to a tenant?

Yes, except for an immediate family member who receives a relative homestead. The Rental and Business Licensing Division, at 763-493-8182, can walk you through it before you sign a lease.

Which school district does my Brooklyn Park address belong to?

Most likely Osseo Area Schools, District 279, but sections of the city sit in Anoka-Hennepin (District 11) or Robbinsdale (District 281). Verify the address before naming a school in an ad.

What can hold up a Brooklyn Park closing?

Unpaid property taxes, which block a transfer until they are cleared, and a buyer's loan approval. A cash buyer with clean title sidesteps the second one.

What should I expect when selling a house in Woodbury?

Woodbury is one of the pricier east metro suburbs, and most sales here involve newer houses, active buyers and a short list of city rules about rentals and permits. The city is eight miles east of St. Paul along Interstate 94 in Washington County, and it is the seventh most populous city in Minnesota.

Because the houses are comparatively young, repair problems tend to be smaller than in older cities. The sellers who struggle are usually the ones with a tenant in place, an inherited house far from family, or a deadline that rules out a showing schedule.

What do the Census figures show for Woodbury?

Woodbury had an estimated 81,558 residents on July 1, 2025, a gain of 8.6% over the April 2020 base of 75,105. It counted 61,961 people in 2010 and 46,463 in 2000, so the city has grown by about 75% since 2000.

  • 29,312 households averaging 2.66 people (2020 to 2024)
  • 77.6% of homes owner-occupied
  • Median owner-occupied home value: $450,200
  • Median monthly owner cost with a mortgage: $2,412
  • Median gross rent: $1,908
  • Median household income: $125,310
  • 61.3% of adults 25 and older with a bachelor's degree, and 5.3% of residents in poverty

Families dominate: 25.8% of residents are under 18, and the 2020 census found children in 38.2% of households and married couples in 59.9%. South Washington County Schools, District 833, is the city's second largest employer after M Health Fairview, which shows how closely local life is tied to the school system.

High values mean a seller's equity is usually large, so the main question is speed and certainty rather than whether the sale clears the loan.

How did Woodbury grow from farmland to a suburb?

The area was first settled in 1844 and was originally called Red Rock before the name changed to honor Levi Woodbury, because another Red Rock Township already existed in Minnesota. It was mostly woods at first and then became farmland, and the township government was organized in 1858.

The first suburban development, Woodbury Heights, broke ground in 1955. Voters turned down a joint incorporation with Cottage Grove in 1963, 1,284 to 662, and then approved incorporating Woodbury alone on February 14, 1967, by 543 to 164. The village was officially incorporated on March 7, 1967. A 2025 estimate of 81,558 shows how far that decision carried it.

What does the land and neighborhood layout look like?

Woodbury covers 35.722 square miles, of which 34.895 are land. Interstate 94 forms the northern edge, 60th Street South the southern, Century Avenue the west and Manning Avenue the east. Neighbors include Oakdale, Lake Elmo, Cottage Grove, Maplewood, Newport and Afton.

The city sits on upland between the Mississippi and St. Croix river valleys. Small lakes dot it, including Powers, Wilmes, Colby and Carver, and the northeast corner drains to Valley Creek, one of the few remaining trout streams in the Twin Cities area. Woodbury maintains 63 parks covering about 3,600 acres and around 180 miles of mostly paved trails, which tends to be a selling point for houses near the lakes.

Climate data for the city show a January mean daily high of 23 degrees and a July high of 83, with about 32.6 inches of precipitation a year. Roofs, gutters and furnaces get tested every season.

What must a Woodbury landlord do before selling a rental house?

Any single family home, townhome or condominium rented in Woodbury needs a city rental license, and the license expires December 31 each year. There is no exemption for owners with only one rental unit. Exceptions exist for family-occupied homes, state-licensed nursing homes, some contract-for-deed sales while the buyer lives there, a fee waiver for owners on active military duty, and small state-licensed residential settings.

Woodbury single-dwelling rental license facts from the City of Woodbury rental licensing pages

Contact651-414-3414 or rental@woodburymn.gov

Applications for 2027 are not open yet and will be available after the City Council adopts the 2027 fee schedule. Mid-year additions are pro-rated by quarter. A buyer who plans to keep a tenant should ask the Code Enforcement Division how the license transfers.

Are short-term rentals allowed in Woodbury?

No. City code prohibits renting a property for a term shorter than 30 days when the renter's permanent residence is elsewhere. That matters for a buyer who is pricing a house on vacation-rental income, and for a seller whose listing history shows nightly bookings.

Tell any serious buyer about past short-term use up front. The disclosure rules ask sellers to share material facts they know, and a code violation fits that description.

Which permits come up when you fix a Woodbury house for sale?

Woodbury uses a combination permit system. One permit covers building, plumbing, heating and cooling, and electrical fees for additions, basement finishes, decks, porches, remodels, repairs and new construction. Stand-alone flat-fee permits cover single replacements such as a furnace, air conditioner, water heater, water softener or EV charger outlet, and they go to the licensed contractor doing the work or to the homeowner.

  • Applications go through the city's online permitting portal
  • Residential contractors must hold a valid Minnesota license or a mechanical bond
  • Morning inspection windows run 9:30 to 11:30 a.m., so call by 9 a.m.
  • Afternoon windows run 1:30 to 3:30 p.m., so call by 1 p.m.

Call the Building Inspections Division at 651-714-3543 if you are unsure whether a project needs a permit. Finish and close any open permits before listing so a buyer's lender does not find them.

What taxes and recording steps apply at a Woodbury closing?

The deed is recorded with the Washington County Recorder. Minnesota's deed tax on a sale above $3,000 is .0033 of the net consideration under Minnesota Statutes 287.21, and it is due when the deed is presented for recording. At a $450,000 price, which is close to the city's median value, that works out to $1,485.

Your title company normally collects the tax and files the deed. Ask for the figure in the closing statement ahead of time, so you are not surprised on the day.

Who employs Woodbury residents, and how do they commute?

The city's 2022 financial report lists M Health Fairview with 1,013 employees, South Washington County Schools (District 833) with 964, Target with 864 and 3M with 759. Many residents also work at 3M's headquarters a few miles west in Maplewood. A large part of local business is retail, centered on Tamarack Village, Woodbury Village and Woodbury Lakes.

The mean commute is 23.9 minutes, and 98.0% of households have broadband. State Farm once employed about 2,000 people in a Woodbury building that opened in 1994; the company moved the work to Lincoln, Nebraska in 2006, and the vacant building was demolished in 2015 for redevelopment.

Do I need a rental license to sell a rented house in Woodbury?

You need one to operate it as a rental until the sale closes. Single family homes, townhomes and condominiums rented in Woodbury all require a license, and the 2026 fee is $80 per unit.

Can a buyer run an Airbnb in Woodbury?

No. City code bans rentals under 30 days when the renter does not live there permanently.

Does Woodbury inspect rental interiors?

Usually not. Owners complete a self-certification checklist each year, and the city inspects inside only for follow-up on a checklist item, an outstanding violation or a complaint.

It is .0033 of the net consideration when the price is above $3,000, which is about $1,485 on a $450,000 sale. The tax is due when the deed is presented for recording.

Which county records a Woodbury deed?

Washington County. Contact its recorder's office for current filing fees, and confirm with your title company who will submit the paperwork.

Why is Lakeville, Minnesota, different from other Twin Cities suburbs for sellers?

Lakeville is the largest city in Dakota County and the ninth most populous in Minnesota, with 79,270 residents in the Census Bureau's July 1, 2025 estimate. It sits about 20 miles south of both downtown Minneapolis and downtown St. Paul along Interstate 35, and it grew 14.1 percent between April 2020 and mid-2025. That pace is the fastest of the four cities in the Census comparison, so sellers here deal with a market that keeps adding new homes alongside resales.

The city covers about 36 square miles of land. J. J. Brackett platted the town site in 1855 on a lake he called Prairie Lake; it was renamed Lake Marion after Marion Savage built the Dan Patch rail line to serve his Antlers Amusement Park in 1910. Lakeville was incorporated as a city in 1967 and stayed mostly agricultural until the interstate and rising metro land costs pulled housing south. Large farms growing corn, soybeans and dairy cattle still operate.

A branch of the Vermillion River, which the state has designated a trout stream, crosses Lakeville, and North Creek, one of its tributaries, starts in the northern part of the city. Winters are cold: weather-station data for 2010 to 2020 show a mean January daily high of 22.6 degrees Fahrenheit and a low of 10.4.

What do Census numbers show about Lakeville homes and households?

Lakeville has the highest home values and incomes of the four cities in the Census comparison. The median owner-occupied home is valued at $452,500 for 2020-2024, and 87.8 percent of housing units are owner-occupied, with 25,685 households averaging 2.89 people.

The $1,806 median rent is the highest of the four, which matters if your house could be rented out as an alternative to selling.

Do Lakeville rental and short-term rental rules affect a house sale?

Yes, if the house is currently rented or you are considering renting it first. Lakeville's council adopted a residential rental registration ordinance in September 2023 for long-term rentals, defined as 32 days or longer. Registration is mandatory, free, and one-time unless contact information or ownership changes, and the city does not require inspections. Owners of several rentals must file a form for each property.

Short-term rentals are allowed only with a Short-Term Rental Administrative Permit under Title 9, Chapter 10 of city code. Highlights from the city's list of requirements:

  • Listings must show the city permit number, maximum occupancy and maximum number of vehicles.
  • Overnight guests are capped at two adults per bedroom plus their dependent children.
  • Guest vehicles must park in the garage or on the driveway, and noise must be reduced between 10:00 PM and 7:00 AM.
  • Owners pay local lodging tax under Title 3, Chapter 17 of city code.

A buyer who wants to run a rental after closing will ask whether the property is registered, so file the registration if you still hold the house as a rental.

What are the ways to sell a Lakeville house on a short timeline?

Lakeville sellers usually weigh a full-service listing against a cash sale. With a median value of $452,500 and 87.8 percent owner-occupancy, most competing homes are single-family houses owned by their residents, so a well-prepared listing can draw several buyers in a city this size.

  • A listing makes sense when the house is current on maintenance and you can accept showings, appraisal timing and the buyer's financing conditions.
  • A direct cash sale fits a house with deferred repairs, a probate or inherited property, or a rental where the lease complicates showings.
  • Selling it yourself removes the agent fee but puts disclosures and negotiation on you.

Cold winters add one condition-related item: in January the mean daily high is only 22.6 degrees, so roof, furnace and insulation condition tend to draw buyer questions. Gather service records for those systems before you open the house to buyers. If the sale involves an inherited house, ask a title company whether the estate needs court paperwork before the deed can be signed.

Which Lakeville school district am I in, and why does it matter?

Most Lakeville households are in Lakeville Area School District 194, which runs two high schools, Lakeville North and Lakeville South, each with close to 2,000 students, plus nine elementary schools and three middle schools (Century, McGuire and Kenwood). Parts of northern and eastern Lakeville fall under District 196 (Rosemount-Apple Valley-Eagan) or Farmington District 192.

Because the boundaries date from the farming era, two neighbors can be in different districts. Minnesota's open enrollment law also lets families choose a school outside their home district. When you write your listing, name the exact district for the address so buyers do not have to guess.

Which employers, roads and areas draw buyers to Lakeville?

Airlake Industrial Park covers about 1,500 acres and holds as many as 200 companies with an estimated 4,500 employees. It is served by Airlake Airport, a reliever airport run by the Metropolitan Airports Commission. Post Consumer Brands has kept its headquarters in the city since 2015. The Minneapolis air route traffic control center sits a few miles away in Farmington.

Interstate 35 is the main artery, and Cedar Avenue (Minnesota Highway 77) runs along the east side. The Census puts the average commute at 23.6 minutes. The Argonne area, a post-World War I settlement project now covered with suburban retail, still appears by that name on maps.

How do I close the Lakeville water account and record the deed?

Lakeville bills residential water quarterly and calculates sewer charges from winter-quarter water use. The city's Form Center has an online stop-service form for sellers and a start-service form for buyers, and you can pay bills through InvoiceCloud, by mail, or at City Hall at 20195 Holyoke Avenue. Call the Utility Division at 952-985-2700 with questions about the meter.

Dakota County Property Taxation and Records records Lakeville deeds at its Hastings office. State deed tax of 0.0033 on a sale at the city's $452,500 median value comes to about $1,493. The county auditor must confirm there are no delinquent taxes before the deed can be recorded (Minnesota Statutes 272.12), and Minnesota Statutes 513.55 requires you to give the buyer a written disclosure of material facts before signing a purchase agreement.

Dakota County's 2026 tax calendar lists May 15 and October 15 as the due dates for the two halves of real estate tax. Late payments carry a 2 percent penalty on homestead property and 4 percent on other property under state law.

More questions about Lakeville, MN

How big is Lakeville compared with nearby cities?

Lakeville is the largest city in Dakota County, at 79,270 people in the 2025 Census estimate. Farmington next door has 25,425 and Inver Grove Heights has 36,873. Its size means a large pool of potential buyers and a lot of new construction competing with resales.

Do I need to register my Lakeville rental before selling it?

Lakeville requires registration of residential rentals of 32 days or longer, with no fee and no inspection. Register each property once, and update the city if ownership or contact information changes.

Can a buyer run a short-term rental in a Lakeville house?

Only with a Short-Term Rental Administrative Permit from the city, and the owner must follow the Title 9, Chapter 10 performance standards. Those include listing the permit number and limiting guests to two adults per bedroom.

How much deed tax will I see on a Lakeville sale?

State deed tax is 0.0033 of the net price above $3,000. On a $452,500 sale, that is about $1,493. Your title company will show the exact figure on the closing statement.

Who do I contact to stop Lakeville utilities when I sell?

Use the Finance forms on the city's Form Center to stop service, or contact the Utility Division at 952-985-2700. Bills are quarterly, so ask for a final read that matches your closing date.

  • Owner-handled sale: you keep the commission and run the negotiation yourself.
  • Direct sale: the house stays as it is, the closing date is quick, and the price reflects the work a buyer takes on.

What does the Census Bureau say about Plymouth's housing market?

The district depends on where the house stands, and Plymouth is split five ways. Confirm the address before printing a school name in an advertisement.

How did Plymouth grow, and does its layout affect a sale?

Plymouth started as a farming settlement on the shore of Parkers Lake in the 1850s. It became a village on May 18, 1955, adopted council-manager government in 1968 and turned into a home rule charter city in 1992 when voters approved a charter.

Farming remained the main occupation into the mid-1900s, and subdivisions followed. The city now maintains about 300 miles of streets and 863 cul-de-sacs, so many houses sit on quiet curving blocks and not on a grid. Medicine Lake and Parkers Lake both lie inside the city limits, and lakeside houses attract their own set of buyers. The city's business welcome page counts more than 80,000 residents and nearly 53,000 jobs, a base of workers who relocate or move up within the west metro.

Winters are cold, with average lows near 3 degrees Fahrenheit. A buyer's inspector will look hard at the roof, gutters, attic insulation and furnace of a Plymouth house, so check those before the first showing.

What should I know if my Plymouth house is a rental?

Every Plymouth rental needs a rental dwelling license, whether it is a single-family home or a large complex. One- and two-family homes and condominium units get a three-year license, and other dwelling types are licensed each year.

City inspectors visit apartment buildings annually and other rental housing every three years. An owner or manager with more than one Plymouth rental has to complete Crime Free Multi-Housing training before renewal. Licenses cannot be transferred or refunded, so a buyer who wants to keep your tenant must apply under the buyer's own name. Call the Community and Economic Development department at 763-509-5430 for the current fee schedule and for the timing of your next inspection.

The city also has a lodging tax ordinance that applies to short-term rentals. If you rented the house by the night, ask the city how that tax applies before you close.

What disclosures and paperwork does a Plymouth sale require?

Before the purchase agreement is signed, Minnesota Statutes section 513.55 has you put in writing the facts you know that could significantly hurt an ordinary buyer's enjoyment of the home. The statement must be made in good faith and reflect what you actually know.

Section 103I.235 adds a well statement. You either list each known well, with its legal description and a map, or state that you know of none. Many sellers can use the short "no known wells" line on the deed, but check the property for an old unsealed well first. At closing, Hennepin County's recording office expects the deed, an electronic certificate of real estate value for any price above $3,000, a "send tax statements to" address and the well statement.

  • Recording runs $46 per document, with a $5 conservation fee added where state deed tax is paid.
  • A deed cannot be recorded against a parcel carrying delinquent taxes, so clear any balance first.
  • Documents can go in by appointment at the Government Center, through your title company's eRecording, on the county's Virtual Recorder site for a $3 service fee, or by mail.

The county's recording page carries the current fee list and a deed tax calculator.

How are Plymouth property taxes handled at closing?

Plymouth's property tax bill from Hennepin County comes due in spring and fall, on the 15th of May and of October. A deadline that falls on a weekend or holiday slides to the next business day. This year's fall deadline is behind us, so confirm that payment posted before you list.

State law adds a penalty to late payments, and the penalty keeps growing each month on the unpaid part. If a lender escrows your taxes, ask the servicer for payoff and escrow refund figures well ahead of closing. The title company then divides the current year's bill by ownership dates. The county's tax payment page explains payment methods, and the property tax line at 612-348-3011 can confirm a parcel's status.

More questions about Plymouth, MN

Can I sell my Plymouth house without making repairs?

Yes, a house can change hands in its present condition. You still owe the buyer a written statement of material facts you know about. Traditional buyers tend to negotiate over inspection findings, while a direct buyer builds the repair cost into the price and closes without asking you to fix anything.

Does the rental license go to the buyer of my Plymouth rental?

No. The license cannot be transferred, so the new owner applies for one. Tell the buyer when yours expires and when the next city inspection falls due.

Which office records a Plymouth deed?

Hennepin County's Recorder and Registrar of Titles, not city hall. Book a time at the Government Center in Minneapolis, mail the deed, have your title company eRecord it, or file online for a $3 service fee.

What if I owe back property tax on my Plymouth home?

The unpaid amount and its penalties must be cleared before the deed can be recorded, usually through the title company at closing. Hennepin County's property tax line, 612-348-3011, can give an exact figure.

How do I find out which school district my Plymouth address belongs to?

Ask the district itself. Wayzata, Robbinsdale, Osseo and Hopkins each cover part of Plymouth, with Wayzata taking most of the city. Have the answer ready before your first showing, because buyers with children will ask.

Which ways of selling work best for a Blaine house?

  • Sell for cash to an investor and skip showings and repair negotiations.

Whichever route you choose, the same Minnesota paperwork applies, and the county that records your deed is almost always Anoka County.

Where is Blaine, and who buys homes there?

Blaine is a fast-growing suburb that sits mostly in Anoka County, with a piece in Ramsey County, and its buyers are mainly commuters and families. The city's own history says the population passed 75,000 by 2025, making Blaine the largest city in Anoka County. The count was 1,694 in 1950 and reached 70,222 at the 2020 count.

The land explains the housing. Sandy soil and wetlands discouraged farming, so dairy and sod farms later gave way to subdivisions. Developers in areas such as The Lakes and Club West dredged ponds and used the sand to raise the building sites, and Sunrise Lake in The Lakes is the largest water body in the city at 158 acres. Laddie Lake, at 77 acres, is the only natural lake.

Main routes are Interstate 35W, Highway 65, Highway 10, Highway 610, University Avenue, Lexington Avenue and Hamline Avenue. The National Sports Center opened in 1990 and the TPC Twin Cities golf course in 2000, and the sports center has more than 50 full-size soccer fields plus an eight-sheet ice arena.

Which school districts serve Blaine homes?

Three districts serve Blaine, and the one tied to your address is a real selling point. Anoka-Hennepin covers most of the city, including the area from Highway 65 to University Avenue north of 99th Avenue NE. Spring Lake Park Schools covers nearly everything south of 99th Avenue NE, and Centennial Schools covers the area east of Lexington Avenue and south and east of Interstate 35W.

The city has Blaine High School in Anoka-Hennepin, Centennial High School, and Paladin Career and Technical High School, a public charter school. Because boundaries run along streets and not neighborhoods, two houses a block apart can belong to different districts. Put the district name in your listing or your conversation with a buyer, and confirm it with the district before you quote it.
